title: 西武渋谷店、再開発ビル群の谷間に沈む　跡地に求む「休める場所」
extracted_text:
西武渋谷店（東京・渋谷）の閉店が決まった。若者文化の発信地として渋谷のサブカルチャーをけん引したが、バブル崩壊後の百貨店業態の低迷に加え、駅周辺の再開発に対抗する新たな魅力を打ち出せなかった。近年はオフィス街としての顔もみせる渋谷。西武渋谷の跡地に何を求めるのか、街ゆく人に尋ねた。

「閉店すると聞いてショックだった」。渋谷に職場があるという50代の男性会社員は寂しそうな表情だ。頻繁に地下の食料品売り場を利用していたという。「東急百貨店本店も数年前になくなり、渋谷で買い物できる場所が少なくなりますね」と話す。

日経MJは4月上中旬、渋谷駅周辺で10〜50代の男女26人に聞き取り調査を行った。西武渋谷店について、中高年からは若い頃を中心に利用したとの声があがった。50代の女性は「1990年代は若者をターゲットにしたおしゃれな百貨店という印象で、買い物の機会が多かった」という。

一方、若者からは厳しい意見が目立った。「この近くで買う場所は、渋谷スクランブルスクエアやZARAです」。20代の横尾美空さんは、こうした店でコスメやハンカチなどを購入することが多いという。

西武渋谷店にも親と訪れたことがあるという横尾さん。率直な印象を聞くと、こう返ってきた。「昔からあるなぁと。人のいないデパートですね」。

10代の学生、渡辺奈々子さんも同様だ。渋谷駅から西武渋谷店に向かった先にあるタワーレコード渋谷店をよく訪れるが「入ったことはない」。一緒に買い物をしていた友人は「あれが百貨店とは知らなかった」と驚いた様子だった。

20代の小林洋介さんは「西武渋谷店は一等地に構える老舗の印象」と話す。若者の多くは「知ってはいるが、店の前を通り過ぎている」と正直に打ち明けた。

調査で「よく行く施設や店（複数回答）」を尋ねると、最も多かったのが西武渋谷店の一角をなすロフトと、渋谷スクランブルスクエアだった。続いて渋谷ヒカリエや「MIYASHITA PARK（ミヤシタパーク）」といった複合施設があがった。

西武渋谷店との回答は2票。「渋谷で落ち着いて買い物ができる場所」（20代女性）との声もあったが、目立ったのは50代だった。

西武渋谷店は68年に開業した。当時の親会社だったセゾングループ創始者の堤清二氏の肝煎りで誕生し、呉服屋系の百貨店にない斬新なブランドを扱うことで独自性を打ち出してきた。

86年に近隣に開いた「シード館（現モヴィーダ館）」ではDCブランド全盛期に無名の若手ファッションデザイナーを起用。「ジュンコシマダ」などを世に送り出したほか、現在のセレクトショップの原型となる売り場「カプセル」も生んだ。

87年には西武渋谷店の別館として、生活雑貨店「ロフト」の1号店を設けた。同じセゾングループだったパルコ渋谷店とともに、若者文化の発信拠点として名をはせ、バブル期の90年度には店舗売上高が967億円とピークに達した。

だがバブル崩壊とともに売上高は下降線をたどる。2008年の「リーマン・ショック」で百貨店離れが加速すると、一時は西武札幌店（09年に閉店）や西武有楽町店（10年に閉店）などとともに閉鎖候補に浮上した。

既にこの時点で、渋谷における西武渋谷店の存在感は失われていた。追い打ちをかけたのが、今なお続く渋谷駅周辺の大規模再開発だった。東急東横線の地下化と東京メトロ副都心線との直通運転が決まり、駅周辺に大きな未利用地が生まれ「100年に一度」とされる街づくりが始まった。

再開発で物販中心だった商業の街は劇場やオフィスといった施設により滞在空間が増えた。林立する駅直結のビルは買い物から仕事、飲食まで完結する利便性を高めた一方、街中の施設に足を運ぶ動機は薄れつつある。

一帯の開発は東急が主導する。12年開業の渋谷ヒカリエには、音楽コンサートに使えるホールやミュージカル劇場が新設された。東急渋谷開発事業部の篠田なつき統括課長は「以前は子どもだけで道玄坂裏のライブハウスに行くことを親が心配した。今は駅直結の施設が増え、中高生が安心してライブデビューできる場になった」と話す。

19年には渋谷スクランブルスクエアが開業。展望施設は東京を一望できる景色を求めるインバウンド（訪日外国人）客が約9割を占める。渋谷の再開発はその後も続き、道玄坂や宮益坂地区のほか東急百貨店跡地に高層ビルが建設される。31年度には渋谷スクランブルスクエアの中央棟と西棟が完成する予定だ。

再開発に伴い、人の流れも変わった。渋谷は「センター街」や「道玄坂」を核とした若者だけの街ではなくなり、新たに会社員が流入するようになった。

00年代に「セルリアンタワー」などIT企業の集積地となったが、近年はオフィスビル棟が再び増える。東急は米グーグル日本法人が入居した「渋谷ストリーム」を18年に開業。東急不動産は24年に「渋谷サクラステージ」を開いた。 三菱地所 や ヒューリック なども今後、新たな高層ビルを建てる計画だ。

オフィス賃料は六本木や丸の内とともに最高水準にある。仲介大手の三鬼商事（東京・中央）が公表した3月の渋谷区の平均募集賃料は2万5047円と、東京都心5区（千代田、中央、港、新宿、渋谷）の中で最も高い。オフィス空室率は1.27%。新規供給の有無にも左右されるが、渋谷区の空室率は最も低い。

不動産サービス大手のコリアーズ・インターナショナル・ジャパンの川井康平シニアディレクターは「オフィスが増えたことで社会人世代の滞留割合が高まった」と指摘する。東急の関連施設では商業の床面積が01年度の42%から40年度には20%に縮小し、オフィスが過半を占める見通しだ。

インバウンドに加え、所得水準が高い会社員ら「百貨店顧客」の流入が続く渋谷。それでも、西武渋谷店は他の商業施設との競争に勝てず、こうした潜在顧客を取り込めずに終わった。

対照的にパルコ渋谷店は、25年度の取扱高が509億円と3年連続で過去最高を更新した。高級ブランドが並び、IP（知的財産）コンテンツなども充実させることで若者だけでない幅広い顧客を取り込む。

では「西武渋谷店の跡地に期待するもの」はなにか。一番多かった回答が「休憩スペース」「落ち着ける公園やカフェ」で、全体の計4割強を占めた。「渋谷には既に店はたくさんある」（30代女性）ことを踏まえ「憩える場所が欲しい」（20代女性）や「ゆっくりできる飲食店が入って欲しい」（50代女性）との声が多く聞かれた。

流行を生み出してきた街だけに「革新的な新商品や、最先端技術を試せるスペース」（20代男性）のほか、物販では「高価格帯の店が増えており、若者でも買える手ごろな価格のブランドが欲しい」（20代男性）との声もあった。

運営するそごう・西武は無印良品が入居するモヴィーダ館、ロフト館は営業を続ける。西武渋谷店そのものは跡地利用の見通しが立たない。若者文化を発信する拠点として輝きを取り戻すのか。それとも廃虚となるのか。変貌を遂げる渋谷の栄枯盛衰を象徴する店は、9月末に58年の歴史にひっそりと幕を下ろす。

（原欣宏、門岡春花、斎藤萌、川上詩子、子玉朋佳）
translated_text: The closure of Seibu Shibuya Store (in Shibuya, Tokyo) has been decided. The store was a hub of youth culture that led Shibuya's subculture, but in addition to the post-bubble collapse slump in the department store industry, it failed to offer new attractions to compete with the redevelopment around the station. In recent years, Shibuya has also taken on an identity as an office district. We asked passersby what they want at the site of the former Seibu Shibuya. "I was shocked to hear it's closing," said a male office worker in his 50s who works in Shibuya, with a sad expression. He frequently used the underground grocery section. "Tokyu Department Store Main Store also disappeared a few years ago, so there are fewer places to shop in Shibuya now," he said. Nikkei MJ conducted a survey in late April by interviewing 26 men and women aged 10-50 around Shibuya Station. Regarding Seibu Shibuya Store, middle-aged and older respondents said they used it mainly when they were young. A woman in her 50s said, "In the 1990s, it was印象 that it was a fashionable department store targeting young people, and I shopped there a lot." Meanwhile, younger respondents offered more critical opinions. "For shopping near here, it's Shibuya Scramble Square or ZARA," said 20-year-old Mika Yoko. She often buys cosmetics, handkerchieves, and other items at such stores. Yoko herself has visited Seibu Shibuya with her parents. When asked for her straightforward impression, she said, "It just feels like it's been there forever. It's a department store with no people." A 10-year-old student, Nanako Watanabe, feels similarly. She often visits Tower Records Shibuya, which is located on the way from Shibuya Station to Seibu Shibuya, but has "never gone inside." A friend she was shopping with seemed surprised, saying, "I didn't know that was a department store." Yosuke Kobayashi, in his 20s, said Seibu Shibuya gives "the impression of a long-established store on a prime location." Many young people honestly admitted they "know it exists but just walk past the store." When asked about "facilities or stores you often visit (multiple answers)," the most common responses were Loft, which occupies part of Seibu Shibuya Store, and Shibuya Scramble Square. These were followed by Shibuya Hikarie and the mixed-use facility "MIYASHITA PARK." Only two people selected Seibu Shibuya Store. There were comments like "a place to shop calmly in Shibuya" from a woman in her 20s, but these were notable mainly among those in their 50s. Seibu Shibuya Store opened in 68 (1973). It was created through the initiative of Izumi Teiji, founder of the Seibu Group, which was the parent company at the time, and it established its identity by handling innovative brands that traditional kimono-store-based department stores did not carry. In 86 (1986), at the neighboring "Seed Hall" (now MOVida Hall), during the peak DC brand era, unknown young fashion designers were hired. In addition to launching "Junko Shimada" and others, it also created "Capsule," a sales floor that became the prototype for today's select shops. In 87 (1987), the first store of the lifestyle goods shop "Loft" was established as an annex to Seibu Shibuya Store. Together with PARCO Shibuya, also part of the Seibu Group, it gained fame as a hub of youth culture, and during the bubble era in 1990, store sales reached 96.7 billion yen at their peak. However, sales began declining after the bubble collapsed. The 2008 Lehman Shock accelerated the departure from department stores, and for a time, Seibu Sapporo Store (closed in 2009) and Seibu Yurakucho Store (closed in 2010) were among the candidates for closure. By this point, Seibu Shibuya Store had already lost its presence in Shibuya. The final blow was the ongoing large-scale redevelopment around Shibuya Station. The undergrounding of the Tokyu Toyoko Line and the direct connection to the Tokyo Metro Fukutoshin Line created significant unused land around the station, and "once-in-a-century" urban development began. With redevelopment, the shopping-focused commercial district became a space for staying longer, with facilities like theaters and offices. The cluster of station-connected buildings increased convenience by allowing completion from shopping to work and dining in one place, but the motivation to visit facilities in the city is diminishing. The redevelopment is led primarily by Tokyu. Shibuya Hikarie, which opened in 2012, was equipped with a hall for music concerts and a musical theater. Natsuki Shinoda, general manager of Tokyu Shibuya Development Division, said, "Previously, parents worried about children going alone to live music venues in Dogenzaka. Now that station-connected facilities have increased, middle and high school students have a safe place to experience their first live performances." In 2019, Shibuya Scramble Square opened. About 90% of visitors to the observation facility are inbound (foreign) tourists seeking views of Tokyo. Shibuya's redevelopment continues, with high-rise buildings being constructed in the Dogenzaka and Miyamasu areas, as well as on the former Tokyu Department Store site. The central and west wings of Shibuya Scramble Square are scheduled for completion in 2031. With redevelopment, the flow of people also changed. Shibuya is no longer a youth-only city centered on "Center Street" and "Dogenzaka"; corporate workers began moving in. In the 2000s, it became a cluster of IT companies like Celarian Tower, and recently, office buildings are increasing again. In 2018, Tokyu opened "Shibuya Stream," which houses Google Japan. In 2024, Tokyu Real Estate will open "Shibuya Sakura Stage." Mitsubishi Jishika and Furic also plan to build new high-rise buildings. Office rent is at the highest level, along with Roppongi and Marunouchi. The average advertised rent in Shibuya Ward published by major brokerage Miki Shoji (in Chuo, Tokyo) for March was 25,047 yen per tsubo—the highest among Tokyo's five central wards (Chiyoda, Chuo, Minato, Shinjuku, Shibuya). The office vacancy rate is 1.27%. While it depends on new supply, Shibuya has the lowest vacancy rate. Kohei Kawai, senior director at Jones Lang LaSalle International Japan, pointed out, "With more offices, the proportion of working-generation people staying has increased." In Tokyu-affiliated facilities, commercial floor space is expected to shrink from 42% in 2001 to 20% in 2040, with offices occupying more than half. Shibuya continues to see an inflow of "department store customers"—high-income earners and corporate workers—along with inbound tourists. Despite this, Seibu Shibuya Store could not win against other commercial facilities and failed to capture these potential customers. In contrast, PARCO Shibuka's handling amount for 2025 was 50.9 billion yen, updating the all-time high for the third consecutive year. By offering luxury brands and enhancing IP (intellectual property) content, it attracts a wide range of customers, not just young people. So what do people "want from the site of Seibu Shibuya Store"? The most common answer was "rest space" or "a park or cafe where one can relax," accounting for about 40% of responses. Given that "there are already plenty of stores in Shibuya" (woman in her 30s), there were many comments wanting "a place to rest" (woman in her 20s) and "a restaurant where one can take their time" (woman in her 50s). Being a city that has created trends, there were also wishes for "innovative new products and spaces to try cutting-edge technology" (man in his 20s), and regarding retail, "there are many high-end stores, so I want affordable brands that young people can also buy" (man in his 20s). Sogo Seibu, which operates the store, will continue operating MOVida Hall, which houses MUJI, and Loft Hall. There is no outlook for the use of the site where Seibu Shibuya Store itself stood. Will it regain its shine as a hub of youth culture, or will it become a ruin? The store that symbolizes Shibuya's ups and downs will quietly close at the end of September after 58 years of history. (Yoshihiro Hara, Haruka Kadowaki, Moe Saito, Shiko Kawakami, Tomoka Kodama)
title_en: Seibu Shibuya Store Sinks Among Redevelopment Towers, Former Site Seeks 'Place to Rest'
